claim: 96 participants were tested in a Y-maze navigation paradigm (29 children with μ = 10, std = 0.49; 22 young adults with μ = 28, std = 4.28; 28 healthy older adults with μ = 73, std = 3.90).
source: We tested 96 participants (29 children, μ = 10, std = 0.49; 22 young adults, μ = 28, std = 4.28; 28 healthy older adults, μ = 73, std = 3.90) in a Y-maze navigation paradigm adapted to study the relative influence of landmark and geometric cues on spatial navigation
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of participants and their demographic characteristics with specific statistical measures.

claim: 79 participants were tested in immersive virtual conditions.
source: 79 participants were tested in immersive virtual conditions, while 17 were tested in the real-world replica, see Supplementary file 2and Supplementary file 3 for participant details
evidence: Direct statement of the number of participants in each experimental condition.

claim: 17 participants were tested in the real-world replica.
source: 79 participants were tested in immersive virtual conditions, while 17 were tested in the real-world replica, see Supplementary file 2and Supplementary file 3 for participant details
evidence: Direct statement of the number of participants tested in real-world conditions.

claim: In the landmark condition, children showed a significant bias toward egocentric responses compared to young adults (p<0.01, φ = 0.56, odds ratio = 15.80).
source: In the landmark condition, we found a significant bias toward egocentric-like responses in children and older adults compared to young adults (Figure 2a; overall Fisher's exact test across the three age groups: p<0.01, Cohen's w = 0.47; children vs. young adults: p<0.01, φ = 0.56, odds ratio = 15.80, odds ratio 95% confidence interval (CI) = [1.94:∞], Cohen's w = 0.48
evidence: Statistical comparison with specific p-values and effect sizes reported.

claim: In the landmark condition, older adults showed a significant bias toward egocentric responses compared to young adults (p<0.01, odds ratio = 14.75).
source: older adults vs. young adults: p<0.01, odds ratio = 14.75, odds ratio 95% CI = [1.88:∞], Cohen's w = 0.45
evidence: Statistical comparison with specific p-values and effect sizes reported.

claim: In the geometric condition, there was no significant difference in strategy preference between the three age groups (p=0.43).
source: In the geometric condition of the Y-maze task, there was no significant difference between the three age groups (Figure 2b; overall p=0.43; children: p=0.28; older adults: p=0.22).
evidence: Statistical test results showing no significant differences between age groups.

claim: The probabilities of making an allocentric response in the landmark condition are 88%, 32%, and 31% for young, children, and older participants, respectively.
source: According to this model, the probabilities of making an allocentric response in the landmark condition are 88, 32, and 31% (for young, children, and older participants, respectively)
evidence: Results from a logistic regression model quantifying allocentric response probabilities.

claim: The probabilities of making an allocentric response in the geometry condition are 99%, 82%, and 82% for young, children, and older participants, respectively.
source: whereas in the geometry condition they are 99, 82, and 82%
evidence: Results from a logistic regression model quantifying allocentric response probabilities.

claim: The interaction effect between age and condition is significant (second differences in children vs. young: Δ = 0.38, p<0.001).
source: The interaction effect is significant (second differences in children vs. young: Δ = 0.38, p<0.001; children vs. older: Δ = 0.067, n.s.).
evidence: Statistical test of interaction effect with specific values reported.

claim: In the real-world landmark condition, older participants showed a majority of egocentric responses (p<0.05, odds ratio = 11.11).
source: We found a majority of egocentric responses in older participants navigating the real-world maze (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a, p<0.05, odds ratio = 11.11, odds ratio 95% CI = [0.79: ∞], Cohen's w = 0.41)
evidence: Statistical comparison showing egocentric bias in real-world conditions.

claim: Older adults required a higher number of trials than young adults to reach the learning criterion in the landmark condition (U = 287.5, p<0.05, r = 0.49).
source: In the landmark condition, older adults required a higher number of trials than young adults to reach the learning criterion of four consecutive successful trials (Figure 3a left; older vs. young adults: U = 287.5, p<0.05, n = 27, r = 0.49, Bayes factor [BF] = 1.97).
evidence: Statistical comparison of learning performance with specific test statistics.

claim: There was no evidence that children and older adults needed more learning trials to reach criterion in the geometry condition compared to young adults.
source: In comparison, there was no evidence that children and older adults needed more learning trials to reach to criterion in the geometry condition compared to young adults (Figure 3a right; children vs. young adults: U = 213.5, p=0.19, n = 26, r = 0.25, BF = 0.56; older adults vs. young adults: U = 141.5, p=0.55, n = 23, r = 0.12, BF = 0.58).
evidence: Statistical tests showing no significant differences in learning trials.

claim: There was a significant main effect of age on traveled distance (F(73,2) = 6.6, p<0.01).
source: There was a significant main effect of age on navigation variables (traveled distance: F(73,2) = 6.6, p<0.01, BF = 1.53, Figure 3b
evidence: ANOVA results showing age effect on navigation variable.

claim: There was a significant main effect of age on escape latency (F(73,2) = 8.7, p<0.01).
source: escape latency: F(73,2) = 8.7, p<0.01, BF = 31, Figure 3c
evidence: ANOVA results showing age effect on navigation variable.

claim: There was a significant main effect of age on orientation duration (F(73,2) = 3.6, p<0.05).
source: orientation duration: F(73,2) = 3.6, p<0.05, BF = 2.37, Figure 3d
evidence: ANOVA results showing age effect on navigation variable.

claim: There was a significant main effect of age on navigation duration (F(73,2) = 8.73, p<0.001).
source: navigation duration: F(73,2) = 8.73, p<0.001, BF = 19.88, Figure 3e
evidence: ANOVA results showing age effect on navigation variable.

claim: There was a significant main effect of age on walking speed (F(73,2) = 3.3, p<0.05).
source: walking speed: F(73,2) = 3.3, p<0.05, BF = 1.94, Figure 3f
evidence: ANOVA results showing age effect on navigation variable.

claim: The condition strongly influenced the distance traveled by participants (F(73,1) = 48.6, p<0.0001).
source: The condition strongly influenced the distance traveled by the participants (traveled distance: F(73,1) = 48.6, p<0.0001, BF = 1.1 × 106)
evidence: ANOVA results showing condition effect on navigation variable.

claim: The condition strongly influenced walking speed (F(73,1) = 27.9, p<0.0001).
source: and their walking speed (F(73,1) = 27.9, p<0.0001, BF = 4.7 × 103)
evidence: ANOVA results showing condition effect on navigation variable.

claim: Evidence for an interaction between age and condition was found for escape latency (F(73,2) = 3.2, p<0.05).
source: Finally, evidence in favor of an interaction between age and condition was found for the time-related variables like escape latency (F(73,2) = 3.2, p<0.05, BF = 1.49; Figure 3c)
evidence: ANOVA results showing interaction effect.

claim: Evidence for an interaction between age and condition was found for navigation duration (F(73,2) = 4.1, p<0.05).
source: navigation duration (F(73,2) = 4.1, p<0.05, BF = 2.56; Figure 3e)
evidence: ANOVA results showing interaction effect.

claim: In the landmark condition, both young and older participants spent a larger proportion of time visually exploring the sky region (U = 986, p<0.0001, r = 0.82).
source: In the landmark condition, both young and older participants spent a larger proportion of time at visually exploring the sky region (Figure 4a; U = 986, p<0.0001, r = 0.82, n = 50, BF = 3311).
evidence: Statistical comparison of gaze behavior with specific test results.

claim: In the geometry condition, participants observed mainly the floor region (U = 856, p<0.0001, r = 0.74).
source: In the geometry condition, conversely, the participants observed mainly the floor region (Figure 4b; U = 856, p<0.0001, r = 0.74, n = 50, BF = 968)
evidence: Statistical comparison of gaze behavior with specific test results.

claim: There was no evidence for an age difference in the time spent gazing at landmarks (U = 119, p=0.30, r = 0.27).
source: Importantly, we did not find evidence for an age difference in the time spent gazing at landmarks (Figure 4a, U = 119, p=0.30, r = 0.27, n = 27, BF = 0.55)
evidence: Statistical test showing no age difference in landmark gazing.

claim: Egocentric and allocentric older participants spent an equivalent proportion of time gazing at the sky region during learning in the landmark condition (U = 84, p=0.96).
source: We found that during learning in the landmark condition, egocentric and allocentric older participants seemingly spent an equivalent proportion of time gazing at the sky region, and in particular at the landmark in front of their starting arm (Figure 4f; U = 84, p=0.96, n = 16, BF = 0.44).
evidence: Statistical comparison showing no difference between strategy groups.

claim: In the geometry condition, egocentric and allocentric older participants gazed at the floor for an equivalent amount of time (U = 13, p=0.90).
source: Similarly, in the geometry condition, we found evidence that egocentric and allocentric older participants gazed at the floor for an equivalent amount of time (Figure 4g; U = 13, p=0.90, n = 11, BF = 0.54).
evidence: Statistical comparison showing no difference between strategy groups.

claim: Allocentric navigators spent about 40% of the trial duration exploring the sky region, with no age effect (U = 49, p=0.95).
source: Gaze dwell-time analyses showed that allocentric navigators spent about 40% of the trial duration exploring the sky region, with no age effect (Figure 5a; Mann–Whitney U test, young allocentric vs. older allocentric participants: U = 49, p=0.95, n = 15, BF = 0.47).
evidence: Statistical comparison of gaze behavior during probe trials.

claim: Allocentric young subjects spent significantly more time gazing at the sky during probe trials compared to learning trials (W = 44, p<0.01).
source: This was about twice the time spent by allocentric participants gazing at the same sky region during learning trials (Figure 4f; Wilcoxon signed-rank test, young subjects: W = 44, p<0.01, n = 9, BF = 16
evidence: Statistical comparison between learning and probe trials.

claim: Allocentric older subjects spent significantly more time gazing at the sky during probe trials compared to learning trials (W = 21, p<0.05).
source: older subjects: W = 21, p<0.05, n = 6, BF = 11
evidence: Statistical comparison between learning and probe trials.

claim: For egocentric subjects, there was no difference in the time spent gazing at the sky area during learning and probe trials (W = 32, p=0.69).
source: These results were in a stark contrast with those with egocentric subjects, for whom there was no difference in the time spent gazing at the sky area during learning and probe trials (Figure 4f and Figure 5a; Wilcoxon signed-rank test, older group: W = 32, p=0.69, n = 10, BF = 0.39).
evidence: Statistical comparison showing no difference between trial types.

claim: When older adults were in the central area of the maze, they spent a longer time gazing at the circle landmark compared to young ones (U = 45, p=0.054).
source: This observation was confirmed by a quantitative analysis showing that when older adults were in the central area of the maze, they spent a longer time gazing at the circle landmark, compared to young ones (U = 45, p=0.054; n = 14, BF = 2)
evidence: Statistical comparison of gaze behavior in central area.

claim: In the landmark condition, older allocentric adults were significantly slower to initiate walking upon opening the eyes compared to young allocentric subjects (F(32,1) = 20.13, p<0.001).
source: In the landmark condition, older allocentric adults were significantly slower to initiate walking upon opening the eyes compared to young allocentric subjects (i.e., the orientation duration was longer, Figure 7b; F(32,1) = 20.13, p<0.001)
evidence: Statistical comparison of navigation performance.

claim: In the landmark condition, older allocentric adults traveled a longer goal-directed distance than young allocentric subjects (U = 49, p<0.01).
source: they traveled a longer goal-directed distance (Figure 7d; U = 49, p<0.01, n = 15, BF = 2.7)
evidence: Statistical comparison of navigation performance.

claim: In the landmark condition, older allocentric adults were slower to reach the goal than young allocentric subjects (F(32,1) = 30.4, p<0.0001).
source: and as a result, they were slower to reach the goal (i.e., larger escape latency, Figure 7a; F(32,1) = 30.4, p<0.0001).
evidence: Statistical comparison of navigation performance.

claim: In the landmark condition, older allocentric subjects spent a longer time (up to 33 s) in the central area of the maze compared to young participants (F(32,1) = 21.13, p<0.001).
source: Coherent with a view-matching strategy in the presence of landmarks, we found that older allocentric subjects spent a longer time (up to 33 s) in the central area of the maze compared to young participants (Figure 7c; F(32,1) = 21.13, p<0.001).
evidence: Statistical comparison of navigation performance.

claim: In the geometry condition, there was no age effect on escape latency during probe trials (F(32,1) = 0.92, p=0.68).
source: In the geometry condition, there was no age effect on navigation during the probe trials. Older adults were as quick as young ones in using an allocentric strategy in relation to the geometry, to make their decisions and to reach the goal, which argues in favor of similar processes governing spatial behavior in these two age groups in the geometry condition (Figure 7a–d and Figure 7—figure supplement 1, escape latency: F(32,1) = 0.92, p=0.68
evidence: Statistical test showing no age effect in geometry condition.

claim: In the geometry condition, there was no age effect on time in the central area during probe trials (F(32,1) = 0.34, p=1).
source: time in the central area: F(32,1) = 034, p=1
evidence: Statistical test showing no age effect in geometry condition.

claim: In the geometry condition, there was no age effect on orientation duration during probe trials (F(32,1) = 0.72, p=0.79).
source: orientation duration: F(32,1) = 0.72, p=0.79
evidence: Statistical test showing no age effect in geometry condition.

claim: In the geometry condition, there was no age effect on traveled distance during probe trials (U = 109, p=0.11).
source: traveled distance: U = 109, p=0.11, n = 21, r = −0.35, BF = 0.97
evidence: Statistical test showing no age effect in geometry condition.

claim: Gaze altitude patterns during orientation in the landmark condition allowed the future spatial strategy adopted by the subject to be reliably predicted (25% hold-out: p=0.05, 88% and 61% correct classification; leave-one-out: 79% correct).
source: We found that gaze altitude patterns during orientation in the landmark condition allowed the future spatial strategy adopted by the subject to be reliably predicted (Figure 8c; 25% hold-out: p=0.05, 88 and 61% of participants using an allocentric or egocentric strategy were correctly classified, respectively; leave-one-out: 79% of the subjects were correctly classified, n = 26).
evidence: Results from predictive modeling showing classification accuracy.

claim: Gaze altitude provided a robust predictor of the experimental condition (25% hold-out: p=0.0001, 97% and 81% correct classification; leave-one-out: 88%).
source: Expectedly, the gaze altitude also provided a robust predictor of the experimental condition undertaken by the subject (Figure 8d; 25% hold-out: p=0.0001, 97 and 81% of participants were correctly classified in the geometry and landmark condition, respectively; leave-one-out: 88%, n = 49).
evidence: Results from predictive modeling showing classification accuracy.

claim: The participant scores along the first principal axis allowed subjects to be discriminated according to their age (t(45) = 6.32, p<0.001).
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) revealed that the participant scores along the first principal axis of the data allowed subjects to be discriminated according to their age (Figure 9a; young vs. older: t(45) = 6.32, p<0.001)
evidence: Statistical analysis of multivariate cognitive data.

claim: The participant scores along the first principal axis allowed discrimination of strategy preference in the older population (t(30) = 3.11, p<0.01).
source: as well as to the strategy preference in the older population (egocentric vs. allocentric: t(30) = 3.11, p<0.01).
evidence: Statistical analysis of multivariate cognitive data.

claim: Egocentric older subjects had lower scores in the perspective taking test compared to allocentric ones (F(33,1) = 4.34, p<0.05).
source: We found that egocentric older subjects, compared to allocentric ones, had lower scores in the perspective taking test (Figure 9b; F(33,1) = 4.34, p<0.05)
evidence: Statistical comparison of cognitive test scores.

claim: Egocentric older subjects had lower mental flexibility scores (B-A difference: F(34,1) = 7.96, p<0.01; B-A ratio: F(34,1) = 9.73, p<0.01) compared to allocentric ones.
source: mental flexibility (B-A difference: F(34,1) = 7.96, p<0.01, B-A ratio: F(34,1) = 9.73, p<0.01; Figure 8c)
evidence: Statistical comparison of cognitive test scores.

claim: Egocentric older subjects had lower contrast sensitivity at high frequencies compared to allocentric ones (8 CPD: U = 187.5, p=0.0042; 16 CPD: U = 184.5, p=0.0029).
source: and contrast sensitivity, especially at high frequencies (Figure 8d; two circles per degree, 4 cycles per degree [CPD]: U = 194, p=0.088; 8 CPD: U = 187.5, p=0.0042; 16 CPD: U = 184.5, p=0.0029, with Bonferroni α = 0.017
evidence: Statistical comparison of visual test scores.

claim: Human spatial cognition has been mainly characterized in terms of egocentric (body-centered) and allocentric (world-centered) wayfinding behavior.
source: Human spatial cognition has been mainly characterized in terms of egocentric (body-centered) and allocentric (world-centered) wayfinding behavior.
evidence: Statement about established characterization of spatial cognition in the literature.

claim: It was hypothesized that allocentric spatial coding develops later and deteriorates earlier than egocentric coding throughout lifetime.
source: It was hypothesized that allocentric spatial coding, as a special high-level cognitive ability, develops later and deteriorates earlier than the egocentric one throughout lifetime.
evidence: Statement of a hypothesis from prior literature.

claim: An apparent allocentric deficit in children and aged navigators is caused specifically by difficulties in using landmarks for navigation.
source: The results show that an apparent allocentric deficit in children and aged navigators is caused specifically by difficulties in using landmarks for navigation while introducing a geometric polarization of space made these participants as efficient allocentric navigators as young adults.
evidence: Main finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Introducing a geometric polarization of space made children and older adults as efficient allocentric navigators as young adults.
source: while introducing a geometric polarization of space made these participants as efficient allocentric navigators as young adults.
evidence: Main finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Allocentric behavior relies on two dissociable sensory processing systems that are differentially affected by human aging.
source: This finding suggests that allocentric behavior relies on two dissociable sensory processing systems that are differentially affected by human aging.
evidence: Interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Landmark processing follows an inverted-U dependence on age.
source: Whereas landmark processing follows an inverted-U dependence on age, spatial geometry processing is conserved, highlighting its potential in improving navigation performance across the lifespan.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the pattern of results across age groups.

claim: Spatial geometry processing is conserved across the lifespan.
source: Whereas landmark processing follows an inverted-U dependence on age, spatial geometry processing is conserved, highlighting its potential in improving navigation performance across the lifespan.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the pattern of results across age groups.

claim: Egocentric strategies rely on spatial codes anchored on the subject's body or the use of visual snapshots of the environment.
source: Egocentric strategies rely on spatial codes anchored on the subject's body or the use of visual snapshots of the environment (Waller and Hodgson, 2006)
evidence: Definition supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Allocentric strategies are grounded on representations that are independent from the subject's position and orientation, akin to a topographic map.
source: whereas allocentric strategies are grounded on representations that are independent from the subject's position and orientation, akin to a topographic map (Burgess, 2008).
evidence: Definition supported by citation to prior work.

claim: A deterioration of neural structures underlying spatial coding during aging would lead to decreased allocentric navigation capabilities in older participants.
source: It has been extensively proposed that a deterioration of neural structures underlying spatial coding during aging would lead to decreased allocentric navigation capabilities in older participants (Colombo et al., 2017; Wiener et al., 2013; Moffat, 2009; Lithfous et al., 2013; Raz et al., 2004; Lister and Barnes, 2009; Davis and Weisbeck, 2015; Driscoll et al., 2005; Rodgers et al., 2012; Ruggiero et al., 2016; Harris et al., 2012; Mahmood et al., 2009).
evidence: Statement of hypothesis from prior literature with multiple citations.

claim: The majority of experimental paradigms used to assess allocentric navigation in humans were based on the capacity of subjects to use landmarks.
source: However, the majority of experimental paradigms used to assess allocentric navigation in humans were based on the capacity of subjects to use landmarks (Wiener et al., 2013; Davis and Weisbeck, 2015; Driscoll et al., 2005; Rodgers et al., 2012; Bohbot et al., 2012)
evidence: Statement about prior research methods supported by citations.

claim: A preference for geometry and a bias toward egocentric strategies were both shown in aging.
source: Besides, since a preference for geometry and a bias toward egocentric strategies were both shown in aging (Bécu et al., 2020)
evidence: Statement about prior findings with citation.

claim: A preference for geometry and a bias toward egocentric strategies were shown in human development.
source: and human development as well (Bohbot et al., 2012; van der Ham et al., 2020; Newcombe, 2019; Nardini et al., 2006; Bullens et al., 2010)
evidence: Statement about prior findings with citations.

claim: The Y-maze experimental paradigm is traditionally used to dissociate egocentric and allocentric navigation in rodents.
source: We sought to test these hypotheses by employing a Y-maze experimental paradigm, traditionally used to dissociate egocentric and allocentric navigation in rodents (Lenck-Santini et al., 2001; Rinaldi et al., 2020)
evidence: Statement about established methodology with citations.

claim: The Y-maze experimental paradigm has been used to dissociate egocentric and allocentric navigation in humans.
source: and humans (Rodgers et al., 2012).
evidence: Statement about established methodology with citation.

claim: Natural, active body and head motion during spatial behavior avoided limitations of joystick-operated paradigms.
source: Natural, active body and head motion during spatial behavior avoided limitations of joystick-operated paradigms, which prevent subjects, in particular older ones, from integrating visual, proprioceptive, and vestibular cues for reorientation and navigation (Mahmood et al., 2009; Adamo et al., 2012; Harris and Wolbers, 2012).
evidence: Methodological rationale supported by citations.

claim: Joystick-operated paradigms prevent subjects, in particular older ones, from integrating visual, proprioceptive, and vestibular cues for reorientation and navigation.
source: which prevent subjects, in particular older ones, from integrating visual, proprioceptive, and vestibular cues for reorientation and navigation (Mahmood et al., 2009; Adamo et al., 2012; Harris and Wolbers, 2012).
evidence: Statement about limitations of prior methods with citations.

claim: Anisotropic geometry eliminates differences between young adults, children, and older subjects in terms of allocentric navigation capabilities.
source: Here, we report experimental evidence in support of above predictions by showing that anisotropic geometry eliminates differences between young adults, children, and older subjects in terms of allocentric navigation capabilities.
evidence: Main finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Age-dependent differences in wayfinding behavior can be ascribed to differences in coding landmarks versus geometrical spatial cues.
source: We show that age-dependent differences in wayfinding behavior can then be ascribed to differences in coding landmarks versus geometrical spatial cues.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The bias toward egocentric navigation in both children and older navigators is conditioned by the spatial cues present in the environment.
source: Our findings suggest that the bias toward egocentric navigation in both children and older navigators is conditioned by the spatial cues present in the environment, questioning the traditional view of a specific deficit for allocentric strategies per se in development and aging.
evidence: Interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The results question the traditional view of a specific deficit for allocentric strategies per se in development and aging.
source: questioning the traditional view of a specific deficit for allocentric strategies per se in development and aging.
evidence: Implication of the findings for existing theories.

claim: The results highlight the need to revisit the classical allocentric–egocentric dichotomy to encompass the role of two dissociable systems (based on landmark or geometry) in governing spatial cognition across the lifespan.
source: Overall, these results highlight the need to revisit the classical allocentric–egocentric dichotomy to encompass the role of two dissociable systems (based on landmark or geometry) in governing spatial cognition across the lifespan.
evidence: Broader implication of the findings for the field.

claim: In the landmark condition, the equiangular maze was surrounded by three distal landmarks with respect to which any position in the maze could be unambiguously defined.
source: In the classical landmark condition, an equiangular maze was surrounded by three distal landmarks with respect to which any position in the maze could be unambiguously defined (Figure 1a).
evidence: Description of experimental design with reference to figure.

claim: In the geometry condition, the angle between two of the three arms was set to 50°, making any location in the maze uniquely determined by its anisotropic geometric layout.
source: In the novel geometry condition, there were no landmarks and the angle between two of the three arms was set to 50°, making any location in the maze uniquely determined by its anisotropic geometric layout (Figure 1b).
evidence: Description of experimental design with reference to figure.

claim: All subjects were disoriented with the eyes closed before each trial.
source: All subjects were disoriented with the eyes closed before each trial, and they were placed at the starting location facing the center of the maze (Video 1).
evidence: Description of experimental procedure.

claim: Four consecutive successful learning trials triggered the start of the testing phase.
source: Four consecutive successful learning trials triggered the start of the second, testing phase, in which no reward signal was given.
evidence: Description of experimental procedure.

claim: The testing phase comprised six trials, with three control trials and three probe trials.
source: The testing phase comprised six trials, in which departure positions were selected among the two non-goal arms: three control trials started from same starting position (arm A) as during learning, while three probe trials started from the arm B (Figure 1d).
evidence: Description of experimental procedure with reference to figure.

claim: If a subject ended up in arm A during a probe trial, the behavior was classified as egocentric.
source: If a subject ended up in the arm A during a probe trial, that is, by making the same body turn at the center of the maze as during learning, his/her behavior during that trial was classified as egocentric.
evidence: Definition of behavioral classification used in the study.

claim: If the subject reoriented in space and ended up in the goal arm C, the behavior was classified as allocentric.
source: If the subject reoriented in space and inferred the position of the target from either the landmark array (landmark condition) or the geometric layout of the maze (geometry condition) and ended up in the goal arm C, the behavior was classified as allocentric.
evidence: Definition of behavioral classification used in the study.

claim: The behavioral classifications were purely descriptive and chosen to permit comparison with previous works.
source: Note that these behavioral classifications were purely descriptive, and that they were chosen to permit the comparison with previous works.
evidence: Clarification of the purpose of the classification scheme.

claim: The behavioral classifications did not mean to capture the nature of processes or representations underlying the associated behavior.
source: They did not mean to capture the nature of processes or representations underlying the associated behavior (Ekstrom et al., 2014; Wang, 2017).
evidence: Clarification with citations to relevant literature.

claim: The result in the landmark condition is in agreement with previous reports on allocentric deficits in children and older adults.
source: This result is in agreement with previous reports on allocentric deficits in children and older adults (Lester et al., 2017; Bullens et al., 2010)
evidence: Comparison of findings with prior literature.

claim: The absence of proprioceptive and vestibular cues that characterize desktop-based virtual reality was not the cause for the egocentric bias in previous studies.
source: while suggesting that the absence of proprioceptive and vestibular cues that characterize desktop-based virtual reality was not the cause for the egocentric bias in previous studies.
evidence: Inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The allocentric deficits in children and older adults described in the literature are linked to a difference in how arrays of landmarks are used to orient and navigate in space.
source: These findings suggest that the allocentric deficits in children and older adults described so far in the literature are linked to a difference in how arrays of landmarks are used to orient and navigate in space.
evidence: Interpretation of the findings in relation to prior literature.

claim: The sensory restrictions that characterize immersive head-mounted display were not responsible for the observed egocentric bias.
source: which suggested that the sensory restrictions that characterize immersive head-mounted display (e.g., reduction of the visual field or image quality) were not responsible for the observed egocentric bias.
evidence: Inference drawn from comparison of VR and real-world results.

claim: In the landmark condition, children and older adults failed to solve the Y-maze task since they mostly adopted an egocentric behavior.
source: In the landmark condition (n=42), children and older adults failed to solve the Y-maze task since they mostly adopted an egocentric behavior.
evidence: Summary of results shown in Figure 2a.

claim: A significant majority of young adults were able to solve the landmark task allocentrically.
source: By contrast, a significant majority of young adults were able to solve the task allocentrically.
evidence: Summary of results shown in Figure 2a.

claim: In the geometry condition, the three age groups behaved similarly, with children and older adults mostly using an allocentric strategy as young adults.
source: In the geometry condition (n=37), the three age groups behaved similarly, with children and older adults mostly using an allocentric strategy as young adults.
evidence: Summary of results shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Learning to orient using landmarks was more difficult for children and older participants compared to young adults.
source: These results supported the hypothesis that learning to orient using landmarks was more difficult for children and older participants compared to young adults.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the learning phase analyses.

claim: Age-related differences in landmark-based behavior were not due to a lack of visual attention to landmarks during learning.
source: Importantly, we did not find evidence for an age difference in the time spent gazing at landmarks (Figure 4a, U = 119, p=0.30, r = 0.27, n = 27, BF = 0.55), suggesting that age-related strategy difference during probe trials did not result from a lack of visual attention during learning.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from gaze analysis.

claim: The longer time spent by allocentric subjects at fixating landmarks during probe trials may reflect cognitive processes related to landmark-based spatial orientation.
source: These findings suggested that the longer time spent by allocentric subjects at fixating landmarks during probe trials may reflect cognitive processes related to landmark-based spatial orientation.
evidence: Interpretation of gaze behavior patterns.

claim: Allocentric older participants might use a cue-based (i.e., view-matching), rather than map-based, strategy.
source: Since the circle was directly in front of the departure position during learning, this suggested that allocentric older participants might use a cue-based (i.e., view-matching), rather than map-based, strategy.
evidence: Interpretation of gaze behavior during navigation.

claim: Allocentric older navigators tended to decrease their walking speed at the center of the maze and eventually gazed at the red circle, unlike young adults.
source: We observed that allocentric older navigators tended to decrease their walking speed at the center of the maze and they eventually gazed at the red circle, unlike young adults (Figure 6a and b and Figure 5—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Observation from trajectory and gaze analysis with figure reference.

claim: The observation of view-matching in older adults was confirmed by quantitative analysis showing longer gaze time at the circle landmark in the central area.
source: This observation was confirmed by a quantitative analysis showing that when older adults were in the central area of the maze, they spent a longer time gazing at the circle landmark, compared to young ones (U = 45, p=0.054; n = 14, BF = 2), favoring an egocentric view-matching strategy with aging.
evidence: Statistical analysis supporting the view-matching interpretation.

claim: In the geometry condition, older adults were as quick as young ones in using an allocentric strategy to make decisions and reach the goal.
source: Older adults were as quick as young ones in using an allocentric strategy in relation to the geometry, to make their decisions and to reach the goal, which argues in favor of similar processes governing spatial behavior in these two age groups in the geometry condition
evidence: Summary of statistical comparisons showing no age differences.

claim: The observed deficits in landmark-based spatial coding were likely linked to difficulties in flexibly processing and reasoning about landmarks.
source: The main conclusion from these analyses was that the observed deficits in landmark-based spatial coding were likely to be linked to difficulties in flexibly processing and reasoning about landmarks (possibly related to perspective taking, mental flexibility/rotation), as well as to a lower capacity to perceive fine details.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from cognitive profiling analyses.

claim: Visual attention, figure memory, and processing speed differences did not seem to play a role in landmark-based deficits.
source: In contrast, visual attention, figure memory, and processing speed differences did not seem to play a role.
evidence: Conclusion from cognitive profiling showing no effects of certain variables.

claim: A minority of subjects (15%) made errors in recognizing the maze shape.
source: We found that a minority of subjects (15%) made errors in recognizing the maze shape and that all subjects had an intact memory of landmarks (Figure 9—figure supplement 3e).
evidence: Results from memory test with figure reference.

claim: All subjects had an intact memory of landmarks.
source: and that all subjects had an intact memory of landmarks (Figure 9—figure supplement 3e).
evidence: Results from memory test with figure reference.

claim: Almost half of the subjects (45%) could not place the landmarks in the correct order.
source: In contrast, the association between the remembered landmarks, maze layout, and goal position was problematic as almost half of the subjects (45%) could not place the landmarks in the correct order
evidence: Results from map drawing test.

claim: 45% of subjects misaligned the landmark array with the maze.
source: and even when they did, the landmark array was misaligned either with the maze (45%)
evidence: Results from map drawing test.

claim: 65% of subjects misaligned the landmark array with the goal.
source: or with the goal (65%).
evidence: Results from map drawing test.

claim: Among the 15 subjects who made at least one error on the drawing, 11 (73%) failed to use an allocentric-like strategy in the testing phase.
source: Among the 15 subjects who made at least one error on the drawing, 11 (73%) failed to use an allocentric-like strategy in the testing phase.
evidence: Correlation between map drawing errors and navigation strategy.

claim: Binding of the landmarks to the cognitive representation of space, rather than the memory of landmarks itself, would underlie the age-related deficits in allocentric-like behavior.
source: Although performed in a very small sample of subjects, these findings supported our conclusions from the profiling data analyses, in that binding of the landmarks to the cognitive representation of space, rather than the memory of landmarks itself, would underlie the age-related deficits in allocentric-like behavior.
evidence: Interpretation of memory test results.

claim: A geometric polarization of the environment removes the egocentric bias in both healthy older adults (>65 yo) and children (~10 yo).
source: The main finding of this study is that a geometric polarization of the environment removes the egocentric bias in both healthy older adults (>65 yo) and children (~10 yo), and it habilitates their allocentric navigation capabilities.
evidence: Summary of the main finding of the study.

claim: Geometric polarization habilitates allocentric navigation capabilities in older adults and children.
source: and it habilitates their allocentric navigation capabilities.
evidence: Summary of the main finding of the study.

claim: This result provides strong evidence that age-related allocentric navigation deficits can be ascribed to difficulty in using a landmark array for navigation purpose.
source: This result provides a strong evidence in support of the hypothesis that age-related allocentric navigation deficits, largely described in the literature (Colombo et al., 2017; Wiener et al., 2013; Davis and Weisbeck, 2015; Driscoll et al., 2005; Rodgers et al., 2012; Bohbot et al., 2012; van der Ham et al., 2020; Newcombe, 2019; Nardini et al., 2006; Bullens et al., 2010), can rather be ascribed to an difficulty in using a landmark array for navigation purpose.
evidence: Interpretation of findings in relation to prior literature.

claim: When geometric information is present and informative about spatial relations, children and older adults become as good allocentric navigators as young subjects.
source: However, when geometric information is present and informative about the spatial relations between the goal and the subject's position in space, children and older adults become as good allocentric navigators as young subjects.
evidence: Summary of the main finding.

claim: All subjects had similar visual exploratory behavior during learning regardless of age.
source: During learning, all subjects had similar visual exploratory behavior regardless of age (e.g., they all gazed at landmarks for equivalent amount of times).
evidence: Summary of gaze analysis results.

claim: The difficulty in using landmarks for navigation is not merely caused by a lack of visual attention to them.
source: This result suggests that the difficulty in using landmarks for navigation is not merely caused by a lack of visual attention to them.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from gaze analysis.

claim: Landmark-specific deficits may be linked to difficulties in spatial manipulations of landmark configurations in a navigation-informative way.
source: The analysis of neuropsychological and cognitive data as well as post-hoc questionnaires showed that landmark-specific deficits may be linked to difficulties in spatial manipulations of landmark configurations in a navigation-informative way (e.g., mental rotation of a landmark array and inference of self and goal positions in relation to rotated landmarks).
evidence: Conclusion from cognitive profiling analyses.

claim: Age-related changes in binding landmark identities to the internal representation of the environment occur, whereas the memory of landmarks themselves was relatively intact.
source: These analyses also suggested age-related changes in binding landmark identities to the internal representation of the environment, whereas the memory of landmarks themselves was relatively intact.
evidence: Conclusion from memory test analyses.

claim: Estimating and reproducing distances and rotations in a geometrically isotropic environment is impaired in older adults.
source: These conclusions are in line with previous studies showing that estimating and reproducing distances and rotations in a geometrically isotropic environment (i.e., a circular arena) is impaired in older adults (Mahmood et al., 2009)
evidence: Comparison with prior literature.

claim: Older adults' performance does not improve when landmarks are provided in a circular arena.
source: and that their performance does not improve when landmarks are provided (Harris and Wolbers, 2012).
evidence: Comparison with prior literature.

claim: Age-related deficits in the retrieval of spatial position of landmarks and their temporal order during route learning have been shown previously.
source: Our data are also in agreement with previous works showing age-related deficits in the retrieval of spatial position (Jansen et al., 2010) of landmarks and their temporal order (Wilkniss et al., 1997; Lindenberger and Baltes, 1994) during route learning.
evidence: Comparison with prior literature.

claim: The observed egocentric bias in aged adults is associated with lower contrast sensitivity to high spatial frequencies.
source: We also show that the observed egocentric bias in aged adults is associated with lower contrast sensitivity to high spatial frequencies.
evidence: Finding from visual profiling analysis.

claim: Lower contrast sensitivity is unlikely to directly cause differences in navigational decisions since landmarks were clearly visible and participants were screened for normal visual acuity.
source: This effect is unlikely to directly cause differences in navigational decisions since landmarks were clearly visible and our participants were screened for normal visual acuity.
evidence: Interpretation of the visual profiling results.

claim: Lower visual scores were repeatedly associated with cognitive impairments in large cohort studies.
source: However, lower visual scores were repeatedly associated with cognitive impairments in large cohort studies (Lindenberger and Baltes, 1994; Roberts and Allen, 2016; Naël et al., 2019)
evidence: Statement about prior research with citations.

claim: Impoverished sensory (e.g., visual) input was shown to increase the risk of cognitive decline in aging.
source: in which impoverished sensory (e.g., visual) input was shown to increase the risk of cognitive decline in aging.
evidence: Statement about prior research findings.

claim: The differential influence of landmark and geometric cues on human navigation suggests a potential dissociation of the related neural processing pathways.
source: The differential influence of landmark and geometric cues on human navigation suggests a potential dissociation of the related neural processing pathways.
evidence: Theoretical interpretation of the findings.

claim: If different subnetworks in the brain mediate the processing of different types of cues, the subnetwork dedicated to geometric processing matures earlier in development and is preserved better in aging.
source: If indeed different subnetworks in the brain mediate the processing of different types of cues (Ramanoël et al., 2022), our results suggest that the subnetwork dedicated to geometric processing matures earlier in development and it is preserved better in aging.
evidence: Theoretical interpretation with citation.

claim: Construction of geometry-based spatial representations could represent the basic mode of spatial learning.
source: Construction of geometry-based spatial representations could thus represent the basic mode of spatial learning, with efficient binding of landmark to the representations of space developing during primary school years and deteriorating early in aging.
evidence: Theoretical interpretation of the developmental pattern.

claim: Efficient binding of landmarks to representations of space develops during primary school years and deteriorates early in aging.
source: with efficient binding of landmark to the representations of space developing during primary school years and deteriorating early in aging.
evidence: Theoretical interpretation of the developmental pattern.

claim: The proposed dissociation between brain systems mediating geometric and landmark processing is not new.
source: The proposed dissociation between brain systems mediating geometric and landmark processing in the brain is not new, and a number of experimental studies and theoretical models addressed this question (Cheng, 1986; Doeller and Burgess, 2008; Sheynikhovich et al., 2009; Julian et al., 2015; Krupic et al., 2015; Julian et al., 2016).
evidence: Statement about prior research with citations.

claim: The age-related aspect of the landmark-geometry dissociation is novel.
source: However, the age-related aspect of this dissociation is novel.
evidence: Statement about the novelty of the current findings.

claim: Landmark-geometry dissociation may follow the neurophysiological distinction between the dorsal and ventral visual processing streams.
source: In a recent modeling work, we have proposed that landmark-geometry dissociation may follow a well-established neurophysiological distinction between the dorsal and ventral visual processing streams (Li et al., 2020)
evidence: Statement about theoretical model with citation.

claim: The dorsal and ventral visual pathways may mediate allocentric and egocentric cue representations.
source: substantiating earlier proposals related to the role of these pathways in mediating allocentric and egocentric cue representations (Burgess, 2006; Nau et al., 2018; Litman et al., 2009).
evidence: Statement about prior theoretical proposals with citations.

claim: In the geometry condition, all age groups had equivalent performance in terms of behavioral and oculomotor measures.
source: The fact that in the geometry condition of the navigation task all age groups had equivalent performance in terms of behavioral and oculomotor measures suggests that children and older adults may not be as bad navigators as previously thought, provided that anisotropic geometric cues are available.
evidence: Summary of findings with interpretation.

claim: Children and older adults may not be as bad navigators as previously thought, provided that anisotropic geometric cues are available.
source: suggests that children and older adults may not be as bad navigators as previously thought, provided that anisotropic geometric cues are available.
evidence: Interpretation of the findings.

claim: Gazing at the floor contributes to the extraction of geometry-related information about the environment.
source: Confirming previous data from a real-world navigation task (Bécu et al., 2020), we show that gazing at the floor contributes to the extraction of geometry-related information about the environment.
evidence: Finding confirmed by prior work with citation.

claim: Geometry permits fast learning of the environmental layout, efficient inference of self-position, and the relative goal location in space.
source: We put forth an important function of geometry for spatial orientation and navigation across the lifespan, permitting fast learning of the environmental layout, efficient inference of self-position, and the relative goal location in space.
evidence: Conclusion about the functional role of geometry.

claim: These findings highlight the necessity to rethink the impact of age on spatial cognition.
source: Altogether, these findings highlight the necessity to rethink the impact of age on spatial cognition and to reframe the classical allocentric–egocentric dichotomy in terms of landmark-geometry spatial processing and coding.
evidence: Broader implication of the findings.

claim: The findings call for rethinking navigational aids and environment architectural designs where older adults and children usually evolve.
source: It also calls for rethinking navigational aids and environment architectural designs where older adults and children usually evolve.
evidence: Practical implication of the findings.

claim: Emphasizing geometric cues could favor navigation of older adults and children and reduce their chance of getting lost.
source: This article suggests that emphasizing geometric cues could favor navigation of these populations and reduce their chance of getting lost.
evidence: Practical implication of the findings.

claim: A limitation of the results is that the exact neural mechanisms mediating the anchoring of landmarks to geometry-based representation of space and how they are affected by aging remain unknown.
source: A limitation of our results resides in the fact that we remain blind to the exact neural mechanisms that mediate the anchoring of landmarks to the geometry-based representation of space and how they are affected by aging.
evidence: Acknowledgment of study limitation.

claim: The interpretations need to be complemented by neuroimaging investigations, possibly with longitudinal follow-up.
source: Our interpretations thus need to be complemented by neuroimaging investigations, possibly with longitudinal follow-up to reduce potential cohort effects.
evidence: Suggestion for future research.

claim: Experiments should aim at differentiating brain areas implicated in geometry vs. landmark processing in humans.
source: As a first step toward this issue, experiments should aim at differentiating brain areas implicated in geometry vs. landmark processing in humans
evidence: Suggestion for future research.

claim: Older age induces a stronger reliance on the external environment in general and on visual information in particular.
source: Finally, given that older age induces a stronger reliance on the external environment in general (Lindenberger and Mayr, 2014) and on visual information in particular (Agathos et al., 2015; Alberts et al., 2019)
evidence: Statement about prior research with citations.

claim: Results from coupling behavioral and neuroimaging will provide novel insight for rehabilitation solutions for spatial navigation in aging.
source: results stemming from the coupling of behavioral and neuroimaging will provide a novel insight for rehabilitation solutions for spatial navigation in aging.
evidence: Suggestion for future research and its potential impact.

claim: A sample of 79 subjects were enrolled in the virtual reality implementation of the study.
source: A sample of 79 subjects were enrolled in the virtual reality implementation of the study: 29 children (range: 10–11 y, μ = 10, std = 0.49, 17 females, 12 males), 22 young adults (range: 23–37 y, μ = 28, std = 4.28, 13 females, 9 males), and 28 healthy older adults (range: 67–81 y, μ = 73, std = 3.90, 17 females, 11 males).
evidence: Description of participant sample.

claim: A power analysis estimated a minimal sample size of 77 to reach 0.8 power for the study design.
source: Based on these parameters, a minimal sample size of 77 was estimated in order to reach 0.8 power for our design (Faul et al., 2007).
evidence: Description of power analysis with citation.

claim: For the real-world experiment, 17 participants were enrolled: 9 young adults and 8 healthy older adults.
source: For the real-world experiment, we enrolled 17 participants: 9 young adults (range: 22–33 y, μ = 27.39, std = 4, 6 females, 3 males) and 8 healthy older adults (range: 66–78 y, μ = 72.40, std = 4, 4 females, 4 males).
evidence: Description of participant sample.

claim: All young and older adult participants enrolled in either the virtual reality or the real-world experiment were part of the SilverSight cohort study.
source: All young and older adult participants enrolled in either the virtual reality or the real-world experiment were part of the SilverSight cohort study (Lagrené, 2019) at the Paris Vision Institute – Quinze-Vingts National Ophthalmology Hospital.
evidence: Description of participant recruitment with citation.

claim: The children were recruited in a primary school in the Paris area.
source: The children were recruited in a primary school in the Paris area.
evidence: Description of participant recruitment.

claim: All screening and experimental procedures were approved by the Ethical Committee CPP Ile de France V (ID_RCB 2015-A01094-45, no. CPP: 16122 MSB).
source: All screening and experimental procedures were in accordance with the tenets of the Declaration of Helsinki, and they were approved by the Ethical Committee CPP Ile de France V (ID_RCB 2015-A01094-45, no. CPP: 16122 MSB).
evidence: Statement of ethical approval.

claim: Adult participants were included based on corrected visual acuity of at least 7/10 and 5/10 in participants younger and older than 70 yo, respectively.
source: Adult participants were included in the study based on the following criteria: (i) corrected visual acuity of at least 7/10 and 5/10 in participants younger and older than 70 yo, respectively
evidence: Description of inclusion criteria.

claim: Adult participants were included based on a Mini-Mental State Examination score of 24 or higher.
source: (ii) a Mini-Mental State Examination score of 24 or higher
evidence: Description of inclusion criteria.

claim: Adult participants were included based on no physical inability in terms of locomoting without assistance.
source: (iii) no physical inability in terms of locomoting without assistance.
evidence: Description of inclusion criteria.

claim: The immersive virtual reality environment was created using the Unity3D game engine.
source: The immersive virtual reality (VR) environment was created using the Unity3D game engine (Unity Technologies)
evidence: Description of experimental setup.

claim: The VR environment was displayed using the HTC VIVE headset equipped with a Tobii Pro VR binocular eye tracker.
source: and it was displayed using the HTC VIVE headset equipped with a Tobii Pro VR binocular eye tracker.
evidence: Description of experimental setup.

claim: The head position in the real space was tracked at 30 Hz by two laser emitters.
source: The head position in the real space was tracked at 30 Hz by two laser emitters placed 9 m away from each other and at a height of 3 m enabling an experimental capture area of approximately 4.0 × 4.0 m.
evidence: Description of experimental setup.

claim: The HTC VIVE headset had a nominal field of view of about 110° through two 1080 × 1200 pixels displays, updated at 90 Hz.
source: The HTC VIVE headset had a nominal field of view of about 110° through two 1080 × 1200 pixels displays, updated at 90 Hz.
evidence: Technical specifications of equipment.

claim: The Tobii eye-tracker recorded eye movements at a rate of 120 Hz.
source: The Tobii eye-tracker recorded eye movements at a rate of 120 Hz.
evidence: Technical specifications of equipment.

claim: The real-world maze walls were made of black Plexiglas acrylic panels that reflected visible light while allowing infrared light to pass through.
source: The maze walls were made of black Plexiglas acrylic panels that reflected the visible light while allowing infrared (IR) light to pass through.
evidence: Description of real-world maze construction.

claim: Body movements in the real-world maze were recorded by an opto-electronic motion capture system at 120 Hz.
source: Body movements were recorded by an opto-electronic motion capture system (10 infrared cameras, model T160) at 120 Hz (VICON Motion Systems Inc).
evidence: Description of motion capture system.

claim: In the equiangular landmark condition, all corridors were 66 cm wide and 190 cm long.
source: In the equiangular landmark condition, all corridors were 66 cm wide and 190 cm long.
evidence: Description of maze dimensions.

claim: In the geometrically polarized condition, all corridors were 66 cm wide and 230 cm long.
source: In the geometrically polarized condition, all corridors were 66 cm wide and 230 cm long.
evidence: Description of maze dimensions.

claim: The maze size in the geometry condition was 1.54 times bigger than in the landmark condition.
source: Overall, the maze size in the geometry condition was 1.54 times bigger than in the landmark condition.
evidence: Quantitative comparison of maze sizes.

claim: The experiment with the virtual maze lasted approximately 30 min per participant.
source: The experiment with the virtual maze (in either the landmark of the geometry condition) lasted approximately 30 min per participant.
evidence: Description of experimental duration.

claim: A nine-point eye-tracker calibration with head fixed was carried out prior to the experimental session.
source: Prior to the experimental session, the headset and the inter-pupillary distance were adjusted for each participant, and a nine-point eye-tracker calibration with head fixed was carried out.
evidence: Description of calibration procedure.

claim: The quality of the calibration was verified at the beginning, halfway through, and at the end of the experiment.
source: The quality of the calibration was verified by using the same nine-point procedure at the beginning, halfway through, and at the end of the experiment.
evidence: Description of quality control procedure.

claim: Whenever the mean angular calibration error exceeded 3°, the adjustment/calibration/verification procedure was repeated.
source: Whenever the mean angular calibration error exceeded 3°, the adjustment/calibration/verification procedure was repeated.
evidence: Description of quality control criterion.

claim: Before every trial, the subject was disoriented by being passively led around the room for approximately 2 min with eyes closed.
source: Before every trial, the following disorientation procedure was performed: the subject was asked to keep the eyes closed and to hold the hands of the experimenter, while being passively led around the room for approximately 2 min (Video 1).
evidence: Description of disorientation procedure.

claim: To verify the effectiveness of the disorientation procedure, the subject was asked to point to a conspicuous room cue.
source: To verify the effectiveness of the disorientation procedure, the subject was asked to point to a conspicuous room cue (i.e., a computer, located near the exit of the experimental room).
evidence: Description of verification procedure.

claim: If the pointing error was less than 90°, the entire disorientation procedure was repeated.
source: If the pointing error was less than 90°, the entire disorientation procedure was repeated.
evidence: Description of verification criterion.

claim: Before undergoing the two experimental phases, the subject had to perform three exploration trials (60 s each), starting from each arm of the maze.
source: Before undergoing the two experimental phases (i.e., learning and testing, see below), the subject had to perform three exploration trials (60 s each), starting from each arm of the maze.
evidence: Description of exploration phase.

claim: The learning phase ended after four consecutive successful trials.
source: The learning phase ended after four consecutive successful trials, defined as the trials in which the subject went directly to the goal without entering the arm B.
evidence: Description of learning criterion.

claim: The testing phase used the following predefined sequence of starting locations: B, A, A, B, A, B.
source: The following predefined sequence of starting location areas was used: B, A, A, B, A, B.
evidence: Description of testing procedure.

claim: Each testing trial ended when the subject stopped for at least 5 s at the end of one of the three arms.
source: Each testing trial ended when the subject stopped for at least 5 s at the end of one of the three arms.
evidence: Description of trial termination criterion.

claim: No reward signal was given during testing trials.
source: No reward signal was given during testing trials.
evidence: Description of testing procedure.

claim: A questionnaire testing the memory of the experimental environment was administered to a subset of subjects (n = 20) tested in the landmark condition.
source: A questionnaire testing the memory of the experimental environment was administered to a subset of subjects (n = 20) tested in the landmark condition.
evidence: Description of post-experiment assessment.

claim: A subject was classified as allocentric if he or she made a majority of allocentric choices in the three probe trials.
source: A subject was classified as belonging to the allocentric category if he or she made a majority of allocentric choices in the three probe trials.
evidence: Description of classification criterion.

claim: In the landmark version of the virtual experiment, one child and one older participant could not have their preferred strategy evaluated as they returned several times to the starting position.
source: In the landmark version of the virtual experiment, the preferred strategy of one child and one older participant could not be evaluated as they returned several times to the starting position.
evidence: Description of data exclusion.

claim: Two subjects were excluded in the behavioral and gaze analyses but pooled with the egocentric group for the visual and cognitive analyses.
source: Those two subjects were excluded in the behavioral and gaze analyses but they were pooled with the egocentric group for the visual and cognitive analyses.
evidence: Description of data handling.

claim: The cyclopean gaze vector was calculated by averaging the data for the left and the right eye.
source: Once the image was displayed in the HMD, the cyclopean gaze vector was calculated by averaging the data for the left and the right eye.
evidence: Description of data processing method.

claim: If the signal from one of the eyes was judged too noisy, the recording from the remaining eye was used.
source: If the signal from one of the eyes was judged too noisy, the recording from the remaining eye was used.
evidence: Description of data processing method.

claim: There were missing eye-tracking data (young adults: 22%; older adults: 27%) due to blinks or loss of pupil tracking.
source: There were missing data (young adults: 22%; older adults: 27%) due to blinks or loss of the pupil tracking.
evidence: Description of data quality.

claim: Fixations and saccades were not separated for the analyses.
source: Fixations and saccades were not separated for the analyses.
evidence: Description of analysis approach.

claim: A generalized linear (logistic) regression model was trained to predict navigation strategy and experimental condition based on average gaze altitude during the orientation period.
source: A generalized linear (logistic) regression model was trained to predict the navigation strategy (i.e., allocentric vs. egocentric) as well as the experimental condition (i.e., landmarks vs. geometry) based on the average altitude of the gaze relative to eye level (in degrees) recorded during the orientation period of probe trials.
evidence: Description of predictive modeling approach.

claim: 25% hold-out validation was used to assess regression performance.
source: To assess the regression performance, we used two cross-validation procedures. First, 25% hold-out validation, in which the model was trained using 75% of the subjects' data and then tested on the remaining subjects' data.
evidence: Description of validation method.

claim: Leave-one-out validation was used to assess regression performance.
source: Second, leave-one-out validation, in which the model was trained on all but 1 subject, whose data were used for testing.
evidence: Description of validation method.

claim: Strategy prediction was assessed only for the landmark condition since there were only two subjects that made egocentric choices in the geometry condition.
source: Strategy prediction was assessed only for the landmark condition since there were only two subjects that made egocentric choices in the geometry condition.
evidence: Explanation of analysis limitation.

claim: Three binary scores were used to evaluate the map sketches: landmark order, landmark placement relative to maze, and goal placement.
source: Three binary scores were used to evaluate the map sketches. They assessed whether the order of landmarks was correct (independently of their position in space with respect to the maze), whether the placement of landmarks relative to the maze was correct (i.e., if the landmarks were drawn in-between the arms and not at their ends), independently of the landmark order, and whether the goal zone was placed in the correct arm and relative to the landmarks.
evidence: Description of scoring method.

claim: Student's t-tests and ANOVAs were used for statistical comparisons on continuous data that passed normality and homoscedasticity tests.
source: Student's t-tests and ANOVAs were used for statistical comparisons on continuous data that passed normality and homoscedasticity tests.
evidence: Description of statistical methods.

claim: Nonparametric tests were used for ordinal data and when normality could not be achieved.
source: Nonparametric tests were used for ordinal data and when normality could not be achieved.
evidence: Description of statistical methods.

claim: Alpha level for statistical significance was set to 0.05.
source: Alpha level for statistical significance was set to 0.05.
evidence: Description of statistical criterion.

claim: A logistic regression model was fit to assess statistical interactions between age and condition in the Y-maze task.
source: To assess statistical interactions between age and condition in the Y-maze task, a logistic regression model (generalized linear model with binomial response and logit link) was fit to the data.
evidence: Description of statistical method.
